title: Rapid Post-Hail Damage Assessment Using Integrated UAV LiDAR, Multispectral and Thermal Sensing
content: Hailstorms can cause substantial structural and physiological damage to commercial forest plantations, potentially necessitating premature salvage harvesting and reducing recovery of higher-value timber products. Rapid, spatially explicit methods are therefore needed to quantify post-hail damage at operational scales. This study evaluated a UAV-based workflow integrating multispectral, thermal, and airborne LiDAR observations over a commercial Pinus radiata plantation affected by severe hail near Casterton, Victoria, Australia. The Normalised Difference Red Edge Index (NDRE) and Normalised Relative Canopy Temperature (NRCT) were evaluated alongside LiDAR-derived Leaf Area Index (LAI) and crown diameter. Spectral and structural information was additionally combined into an Integrated Canopy Condition Index (ICCI; NDRE × LAI) and an RGB-based variant (ICCIG; GLI × LAI). Expert mapping provided reference classifications of low, medium and severe crown damage. Across 151,022 trees retained in the expert-reference analysis, NDRE was the strongest standalone indicator of damage, declining from a mean of 0.651 under low damage to 0.398 under severe damage and achieving an AUC of 0.954 for severe-damage discrimination. NRCT showed relatively weak discrimination alone, although its addition to NDRE produced a modest improvement under the primary spatial cross-validation. This advantage was not maintained under more stringent directional spatial validation, reinforcing NDRE as the more robust predictor. Adding LAI and crown diameter provided little improvement over NDRE alone. When fitted and evaluated against the complete reference dataset, ICCIG outperformed ICCI in direct classification, achieving 74.2% overall accuracy and 69.1% balanced accuracy. Most errors occurred between adjacent severity classes, with severe damage most reliably identified. Tree-level probability mapping reproduced the principal spatial damage gradient and identified uncertainty within transition zones. The results show that UAV remote sensing can provide a reproducible, spatially explicit framework for post-hail plantation assessment, with NDRE providing the dominant discriminatory information and relative canopy temperature providing modest incremental predictive value.
